name: Erik Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, 27, and most mornings start with a van full of tools and a message from a shop that needs its power back. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I lead the repair work at our small firm. I earn typical pay, rent with my partner Lida, have no children, and keep two months of expenses saved. I use the firm's approved AI note tool daily, but the satisfying part is still finding the fault behind the cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, then I'll keep the bits that save time and stop reading the grand predictions at breakfast. The tool I use to sort my work notes is useful even if nothing bigger follows. Nobody needs a revolution to find a missing receipt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can pay my share of the rent and I've got two months of expenses saved. The pay is ordinary, but I'm good at the work and there are a few other firms within reach. That picture doesn't make me fear for my job or wish I'd chosen another trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the home repair calls and checking installations in small businesses. Starting now I'd carry on using my daily note tool to sort job notes, then check them against what I actually tested. Through the first year I'd use the same approach rather than spend my cushion on speculative equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little disappointment because I enjoy trying things. A slower world still has real faults to find. I'd be glad I hadn't borrowed money just to look modern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check when you use the note tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether each room name and test result is the one I wrote down. I don't put customer details into an unapproved tool, and I use the firm's approved system for work notes. The machine can arrange my words; it doesn't sign my test results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner think of all the experiments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Lida laughs when I spend longer comparing tools than doing the little task. We have no children, but we still have a rent payment every month. I keep experiments inside spare money, not the account for household bills.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** without needing a dramatic story about the future.
I'd value a tool that finds a **receipt** even if larger AI promises come to little.
think: I can cover **rent**, have two months saved, and see some other local employers if needed.
My **repair skills** leave me confident about this job in a world with little radical change.
do: Keep leading **home repairs** and checking small-business installations through the first year.
Continue sorting **job notes** daily with the approved tool, checking every test result myself.
feel: **Calm**, with mild disappointment that fewer new things may be worth trying.
S0.quote: Nobody needs a revolution to find a missing receipt.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** serves checked notes, while safety decisions and recorded test results remain his own responsibility.
The **two-month cushion** supports present calm because bills are covered and experiments stay outside household and emergency money.

steps.text: Keep repair leadership and daily checked job notes in the approved tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should try faster material lists, but we ought to compare mistakes as well as minutes saved. I'll happily be the person who tests a new tool. I won't tell the apprentice a neat list means the circuit is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This would change the quote desk before the screwdriver work. I can see the owner using the saved time to squeeze our paid hours, and my own hours could be among them if the repair diary thinned. I'm interested in the tools and still worried about the wage; enjoying one doesn't settle the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner now for a four-week trial of AI-drafted materials lists on our normal repair jobs. I'd compare each list with my checked list before any order, using existing software rather than buying a subscription myself. During the first year I'd record my paid hours monthly and start checking posted repair vacancies if my hours fell below what covers my share of rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I want to get close enough to understand the change. Staring at an advert wouldn't tell me whether the tool misses a fitting. A trial gives me facts, even if the facts aren't flattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the owner at the end of four weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The number of missing or wrong items and the actual checking time, beside any ordering time saved. I wouldn't hide a bad result because I suggested the experiment. A useful AI trial can end with us deciding not to use the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would trigger the vacancy search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down the paid hours needed to cover my own rent share and ordinary bills. If the monthly hours fell below that, I'd look at real adverts before drawing down savings for long. I wouldn't quit on the strength of an interesting trial.

say: I'd test **materials lists** by comparing errors and checking time as well as speed.
I'd tell the **apprentice** that a neat list says nothing about whether a circuit is safe.
think: My **paid hours** could be squeezed if faster planning meets a thinner repair diary.
I enjoy **new tools**, but that doesn't remove concern about what I'll earn.
do: Request a **four-week trial** now using existing software and manually checked materials lists.
Record **paid hours** monthly through the first year.
Check posted **repair vacancies** if hours no longer cover my share of rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, while eager to understand the tool through a controlled trial.
S1.quote: A useful AI trial can end with us deciding not to use the tool.
fieldNote: His **adaptive approach** includes early testing and willingness to reject a tool, rather than treating enthusiasm as proof of financial safety.
The **job-search trigger** is an explicit household-income threshold; he keeps existing work while examining actual vacancies.

steps.text: Trial AI materials lists for four weeks with owner permission and manual checking
Check posted repair jobs if paid hours fail to cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner we should use the two years rather than spend them arguing about whether the card is possible. Thinking AI arrives in 2028 and hands-on robots follow around 2031. I'd want the apprentice to hear both dates, not just the one that makes our trade sound safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paperwork isn't what makes me valuable now, so I don't expect every repair call to disappear in 2028. Robots in 2031 could still reduce my hours, and some nearby firms could cut back together. Two months saved gives me a start, not enough room to gamble our rent on buying a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd increase my saving by 80 a month now by stopping hobby electronics purchases. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repair work and learn the firm's new planning system if we actually adopted one, using paid work time agreed with the owner. I'd also check posted building-maintenance roles monthly, applying only where stated pay and paid hours covered our bills before considering any move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the things I learn quickly may be exactly what powerful software learns first. I've still got a plan and enough time to make some deposits. I'd want my partner in the conversation before I spent a penny on equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot to compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from two months of household savings. I'd want a real purchase price, insurance costs, actual demand and my partner's agreement before even considering it. Being quick to try software doesn't mean I can afford a machine that doesn't earn its keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does learning on paid time mean here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner to put training inside my paid week if the firm changes systems. If that wasn't agreed, I wouldn't quietly assume free evenings could replace every task. The first step is asking what is really being introduced, not buying a course for an imagined system.

say: I'd explain **both dates** to my partner and apprentice rather than call physical work permanently safe.
I'd use the **two years** to prepare instead of arguing about the scenario's likelihood.
think: I expect **physical repair calls** to remain after 2028, with later robots threatening my paid hours.
My **two-month reserve** cannot fund a robot gamble while keeping the rent secure.
do: Save an extra **80 monthly** now by stopping hobby electronics purchases.
Learn any adopted **planning system** after 2028 only with agreed paid training time.
Check **maintenance vacancies** monthly after 2028 and apply only for sufficient stated pay and paid hours.
feel: **Anxious** about earnings and rapidly changing knowledge, while retaining a practical plan.
S2.quote: Being quick to try software doesn't mean I can afford a machine that doesn't earn its keep.
fieldNote: His **robot caution** follows the actual cushion and household responsibilities despite his appetite for early software experiments.
The **first-year learning** depends on a system actually adopted and agreed paid time; no course enrolment or machine purchase is implied.

steps.text: Save 80 extra monthly by stopping hobby electronics purchases
Learn an adopted planning system after 2028 only with agreed paid training time
Apply after 2028 for posted maintenance roles with sufficient pay and paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years makes a careful experiment possible without turning the house upside down. I'd keep learning useful tools while earning as an electrician. Robots around 2034 are still part of the story, even if thinking AI in 2031 is the first date people discuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my earnings can hold over the next few years while hands-on repair demand stays strong. Five years lets me try a small sideline before relying on it. I don't think a small business is beyond AI or robots; I want another way of getting paid, with losses I can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd set aside 25 a month from spare spending for a small weekend service assembling simple shelves and furniture for neighbours. Once I'd saved 150 for basic non-electrical tools and checked whether my employment terms and local requirements allowed it, I'd advertise two Saturday slots a month. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep my electrical job and continue the sideline only if actual payments exceeded its costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about where the trade ends up, but interested in something I can test cheaply. I'd feel worse if I called it my rescue before the first customer paid. Five years means I can discover a poor idea without staking the flat on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a service outside electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People on our building's noticeboard sometimes ask for help assembling ordinary flat-pack furniture. I've helped family do that, and it doesn't need me to buy a van or electrical stock. I wouldn't offer electrical work under a casual furniture advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months with no paying bookings, or costs exceeding what customers actually paid. I'd stop spending and keep the ordinary job rather than tell myself the next advert would fix it. My partner would see the same little account book I used.

say: I'd use **five years** for a careful experiment while continuing paid electrical work.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** in view when people discuss thinking AI arriving in 2031.
think: I expect **near-term earnings** to hold while repair demand remains strong.
I want a **small sideline** with limited losses, without assuming a business escapes eventual automation.
do: Set aside **25 monthly** now from spare spending towards a 150 basic furniture-assembly tool budget.
Advertise two **Saturday slots** monthly only after saving the budget and checking employment terms and local requirements.
Keep my **electrical job** after 2031 and continue the sideline only while payments exceed costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about the longer trade outlook, with interest in a small and reversible experiment.
S3.quote: Five years means I can discover a poor idea without staking the flat on it.
fieldNote: The **sideline** is bounded by a saved budget, required checks, limited advertised hours and an explicit stop rule based on actual receipts.
He expects **continued near-term repair demand**, while admitting a furniture service is also exposed to the eventual hands-on robot endpoint.

steps.text: Offer two monthly furniture-assembly slots after saving 150 and completing employment and requirements checks
Keep the electrical job after 2031 while testing actual sideline earnings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives me time to make mistakes that are small enough to learn from. I'd still check a tool before asking the apprentice to trust it. A long runway isn't a reason to borrow for every bright idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and money feel secure over the next few years if I keep the limits we've talked about. I'd be 37 in 2036 and about 40 when robots followed, so I'd still need a living afterwards. I'm not confusing a comfortable present with a guarantee for the rest of my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the daily checked work-note tool and keep adding to my normal savings now. I'd test the same furniture service only after saving its 150 budget and checking the requirements, stopping if payments failed to cover costs. In the first year after 2036 I'd review my actual electrical wages and any sideline receipts each quarter before taking on new business costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for now, and curious. I like having time to try something without pretending the whole future depends on one Saturday booking. Robots arriving around 2039 are a reminder to review my plan, not permission to spend the emergency reserve today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your partner agree before spending more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look at three months of actual receipts, costs and my electrical wages. Any extra purchase would have to come from spare money and leave the emergency savings alone. I wouldn't tell my partner a hopeful booking was already income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a successful sideline make you leave electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not automatically. I'd compare real earnings over time and ask whether I even liked doing it every week. Your picture gives robots the ability to do physical work too, so owning the customer list isn't a promise that the service lasts forever.

say: I'd use **ten years** to learn from small mistakes rather than borrow for every idea.
I'd keep checking **tools** myself before asking the apprentice to rely on them.
think: My **near-term work and money** feel secure when experiments stay within affordable limits.
I'll need a living well after **2036**, and present comfort doesn't guarantee a whole career.
do: Continue **checked work notes** and ordinary saving now.
Try the **furniture service** only after saving 150 and completing checks, stopping if receipts fail to cover costs.
Review **wages and receipts** quarterly after 2036 before adding business costs from spare money.
feel: **Calm** about present finances, with curiosity and clear limits on experiments.
S4.quote: Robots arriving around 2039 are a reminder to review my plan, not permission to spend the emergency reserve today.
fieldNote: His **calm assessment** is limited to the next few years and rests on covering bills while keeping experiments outside emergency money.
The **quarterly review** counts actual receipts and costs; he neither assumes a successful sideline nor treats customer ownership as protection from robots.

steps.text: Keep daily checked work notes and review actual wages after 2036
Continue ordinary saving from wages now
Test furniture assembly only after saving 150 and completing required checks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robots follow around 2031, before I could build much extra cushion. Agreed paid training time on systems the firm actually adopts would help. I'd also value real vacancy adverts with paid hours and clear costs for any tool somebody wants me to buy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how much money people can afford to lose while learning. An experiment is only small if the rent still gets paid. I like new things, but my partner shouldn't have to finance my excitement.

headlineQuote: An experiment is only small if the rent still gets paid.
portrait: Erik is **27**, a highly skilled electrical repair lead with a technical diploma and master's licence, typical pay and two months saved.
He rents with his **partner**, has no children, and uses an approved AI note tool daily while checking safety information himself.
His **early adoption** includes measured trials, with pay-hour thresholds and agreed paid training rather than assumed income from faster software.
Longer horizons permit a **limited sideline**, funded from spare spending and checked against actual receipts, without claiming immunity from robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives little time to enlarge his cushion before capable robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Agreed **paid training time** on systems the firm adopts would let him learn while maintaining income.
Honest **vacancy hours** and clear equipment costs would support decisions based on actual money rather than hopeful claims.
